title: History and Evolution of REST
learning_outcomes: Explain how history and evolution of rest affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from origins of rest to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on history and evolution of rest in rest architectural principles. You will connect origins of rest to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: History and Evolution of REST matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying origins of rest deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 19 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 19: Origins of REST → Roy Fielding's architectural model → REST and HTTP's evolution → Modern API design conventions.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: REST is an architectural style with constraints; an HTTP JSON API can be useful without satisfying every REST constraint. In this lesson, treat “History and Evolution of REST” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Concepts to connect
items: REST describes constraints, not a wire protocol

content_blocks.expected_output: The identifier names a resource and the response transfers one representation of its current state.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Origins of REST”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Roy Fielding's architectural model” and “Modern API design conventions”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Describe the architectural choice precisely; do not call every JSON endpoint strict REST. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating history and evolution of rest. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Origins of REST” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for History and Evolution of REST with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating history and evolution of rest as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: REST is an architectural style with constraints; an HTTP JSON API can be useful without satisfying every REST constraint. In this lesson, treat “History and Evolution of REST” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 20: Resources and Resource Identification.
